progression.startsWith: Last time, we named sodium chloride as ions, and carbon dioxide as atoms sharing electrons. But these aren't two separate worlds. Remember our tug of war from the electronegativity video, with two atoms pulling on a shared pair of electrons. If the pull is even, the pair stays in the middle. If one atom pulls harder, the pair shifts toward it. And if one atom pulls much, much harder, it can take the electrons completely. Let's see how that one idea connects covalent and ionic bonding.

teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry M1 V21: Electronegativity and the bonding spectrum. How does electron attraction connect ionic and covalent bonding? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom in a bond attracts the shared electrons. It rises toward the top right of the periodic table. Fluorine is the highest, at four point zero. Chlorine is three point two, hydrogen two point two, and sodium only zero point nine. What decides the bond is the difference between the two atoms' values. Start with two chlorine atoms. Each has seven outer electrons, and needs one more. So they share a pair, one electron from each. That shared pair is a covalent bond. Both atoms pull equally, because the difference is zero, so the pair sits exactly in the middle. That's a non-polar covalent bond. Now hydrogen and chlorine. The difference is three point two minus two point two, which is one point zero. Chlorine pulls harder, so the shared pair spends more of its time near the chlorine. The chlorine end gets a small negative charge, and the hydrogen end a small positive charge. We write these as delta minus and delta plus, where delta means partial, a bit less than a full charge. This is a polar covalent bond.

teaching.openingDecision: opens on v20's final frame (Decisions). On the second sentence the "?" between the cards fades and the rope line grows across the centre; the two cards shrink to the top corners. On "electrons" two nuclei with shell rings appear at the rope's ends, the blue pair on the rope. On the fourth sentence the pair sits centred. On the fifth sentence it slides a little to the right. On "completely" it leaves the rope and joins the right atom's outer ring; the rope fades; the atoms gain "+" and "−". On "bonding" the scene rewinds to a centred pair, and the heading writes on: "Electronegativity: one pull, from sharing to transfer".
teaching.understandingCheck: Quick prediction. In hydrogen fluoride, the difference is four point zero minus two point two, which is one point eight. By the guide, that's ionic. So is hydrogen fluoride made of ions? Have a think. Your turn. Using the electronegativity values given, classify the bonds potassium to chlorine, nitrogen to hydrogen, and bromine to bromine, as non-polar covalent, polar covalent or ionic. For any polar bond, show which atom is delta minus. Pause here to answer. Last one. Draw Lewis dot diagrams for sodium oxide, showing the transfer of electrons, and for ammonia, N H three. Pause here to answer.

Status: Revision 2 (7 Nov 2026): brief 179 learning review and science check clean at Revision 1, so no repair or repair check was needed (root); headline count restated as the sum of scene strings. Ready to voice. Previously Revision 1 (5 November 2026): first design. Needs independent learning review and science check before voicing.

Narration 6,312 characters (sum of scene strings; 6,330 with joining spaces), 19 scenes, about 563 s, counted by script with the build parser rules (see "Narration length estimate"). Nothing recorded; human listening pending. Voice: the Google voice (all Year 11).

Scope: twenty-first video of Year 11 Chemistry (2017 syllabus), Module 1; the first bonding video. It builds on `chem-y11-m1-v14.md` (electronegativity defined as how strongly an atom in a covalent bond attracts the shared pair, the Pauling values, the tug-of-war analogy, the trend toward the top right), `chem-y11-m1-v19.md` (ion charges, MgCl₂) and `chem-y11-m1-v20.md` (ionic against covalent names; its final frame) without re-teaching them. Templates: `phys-y11-fa1-v01.md` (structure), `math-a12-d10.md` (calculation layout for the Δχ steps), `bio-y11-fa1-v05.md` (plates), `chem-y11-m1-v17.md` (series conventions). No starter pack exists; the pack work is done here. Route entry: `chem-y11-m1-v21` in `../../programme/chem-y11-route-inputs.json`. Site lessons read in full (5 November, read-only): `C:/Users/kygs/hscscience/subjects/chemistry/year11/module1/lesson18.sa.html` (SHA256 `018b9247bc9bec32c086f50e45e791b0226ac4ef0dd4dab569d67bdb4b2aac36`, recomputed, matches; used: `l18-using-electronegativity-difference-to-classi-title` and its `-b` twin (the |Δχ| table with thresholds and examples H₂, Cl₂, HCl, NaCl, MgO, KF; "The 1.7 threshold is a guide, not a sharp boundary"; δ+ and δ− placement), Worked Example 1 (Na–Cl, N–H), the HF predict-and-reveal (1.8, yet a polar covalent molecule), the δ− misconception ("Putting δ− on the less electronegative atom"), drill 2 (H–Cl); the reactivity sections were v14 and v15's; the polar-molecule note "A polar bond is not the same as a polar molecule" is v23's) and `.../module1/lesson19.sa.html` (SHA256 `bf0c603459da030fe0c3d036c87ccb0efdfaaed2b1b89235f5d6ae1894d8a025`, recomputed, matches; used: `l19-lewis-dot-diagrams-title` in full (valence electrons only, ionic transfer for NaCl with square brackets and charges, covalent sharing for H₂O with two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, hydrogen's duet, the drawing steps) and Short Answer Q8(b) (MgCl₂ Lewis diagram)). Site corrections file checked: no logged item touches lessons 18 or 19.

Owner rules applied: one learner question; no people, hands or faces (the tug of war is a rope line between two nuclei, as in v14, with no figures); real objects as painted plates where they carry the idea (salt crystals in the handoff); atoms, shared pairs, Lewis diagrams and the spectrum bar coded in the HSC convention; 3 s prediction countdown; "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; brief feedback with one crossed mistake; original HSC-style questions; optional key notes; Australian spelling; no em dashes; nothing in the bottom 12% of the frame. Each Δχ step is a short task strip, the two values as grouped givens, one subtraction, one classification.

Syllabus content (Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 1; local ledger IDs `C1-IQ4-01` and `C1-IQ4-02`), quoted from `../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y11.json`:

- "investigate the role of electronegativity in determining the ionic or covalent nature of bonds between atoms" (this video)
- "investigate the differences between ionic and covalent compounds through:"
  - "using nomenclature, valency and chemical formulae (including Lewis dot diagrams) (ACSCH029)" (Lewis dot diagrams here; nomenclature and formulae in v19 and v20)
  - "examining the spectrum of bonds between atoms with varying degrees of polarity with respect to their constituent elements’ positions on the periodic table" (this video)
  - "modelling the shapes of molecular substances (ACSCH056, ACSCH057)" (v23)

Source: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-03/chemistry-stage6-syllabus-word.docx (page 38)

**Boundary:** opens on v20's final frame. Recalls v14's electronegativity and tug of war in two sentences. Teaches the electronegativity difference (Δχ, spoken "difference") as the cause of bond type; equal sharing (Cl₂, non-polar covalent); unequal sharing (HCl, polar covalent, δ+ and δ− defined); transfer (NaCl, ionic bond as the attraction between oppositely charged ions); the spectrum with the 0.4 and 1.7 guide values and periodic-table positions; HF as the boundary case (1.8 but molecular); Lewis dot diagrams (valence dots only; NaCl and MgCl₂ transfer with brackets and charges; covalent bonding pairs and lone pairs in H₂O; a double bond in CO₂); the answer (one tug of war, two ends). Stops before the lattice and its properties (v22, the handoff), molecular shape and whether a molecule is polar (v23), metallic bonding (v24), intermolecular forces (later), and formal charge or expanded octets (author note d).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How does electron attraction connect ionic and covalent bonding?" The answer, in order: the difference in pull decides where the bonding electrons sit (1, 2); equal pull shares evenly (3); a bigger difference shares unequally (4); a big difference transfers (5); so the bond types are one spectrum (6, 13); Lewis diagrams show the sharing or transfer (9 to 12).
- **Opening frame (equals v20's final frame).** At the left a card "NaCl: sodium chloride" with small teal "Na⁺" and "Cl⁻" tags; at the right a card "CO₂: carbon dioxide" with a small C and O sharing a pair of blue dots, tag "shared electrons"; between them a faint "?" and v14's grey tug-of-war rope line with a blue pair of dots, tag "pull on electrons: electronegativity (v14)"; the chip "Next: how does electron attraction connect ionic and covalent bonding?". Scene 1 enlarges the rope between the cards.
- **Tug of war continued from v14 (analogy).** v14 used it for one shared pair. Here the rope's pair slides with the difference: centred (Cl₂), off-centre (HCl), pulled clear (NaCl). The limit is stated in "Memory aid check" (in an ionic bond nothing is "shared" any more; the ions then attract as whole charges).
- **Values (site, one decimal, as v14).** F 4.0, O 3.4, Cl 3.2, N 3.0, Br 3.0, C 2.6, H 2.2, Mg 1.3, Na 0.9, K 0.8 (Pauling; author note a). Each Δχ is a subtraction on screen, larger minus smaller.
- **Thresholds as a guide (site caveat kept in learner copy).** "below about 0.4 non-polar covalent; 0.4 to 1.7 polar covalent; above about 1.7 ionic", shown as faint bands on a continuous bar, never as walls. The caveat stays in learner copy because without it HF would be taught wrongly.
- **HF as the prediction (site predict-and-reveal).** Δχ = 1.8 but HF is molecular; evidence given: it boils at about 20 °C, while salt melts at 801 °C (author note b). The point: the guide values are approximate; use the evidence.
- **Periodic-table positions (syllabus example).** Scene 6 shows metal (bottom left) with non-metal (top right) as far apart in electronegativity, so ionic; two non-metals close together, so covalent.
- **Lewis dot diagrams (site section).** Dots for each atom's outer electrons; the moving or shared electrons are drawn in amber so their path can be followed (open decision 2 offers dot-and-cross). Ionic: square brackets with the charge outside, metal with no dots. Covalent: a bonding pair between atoms, often drawn as a line; lone pairs named. MgCl₂ links to v19's formula. CO₂'s double bonds are included because v20 named it and v23 needs CO₂'s structure; scene 12 is short.
- **Memory aid:** "Small gap, share. Big gap, transfer." Checked in "Memory aid check".
- **Attempts (original wording, HSC style).** A1: classify K–Cl, N–H and Br–Br with given values, and label δ− for any polar bond (3 marks). Answers ionic (2.4), polar covalent (0.8, δ− on N), non-polar covalent (0). Crossed: "δ− on H". A2: Lewis dot diagrams for sodium oxide (showing transfer) and ammonia (4 marks). Crossed: "Na and O sharing a pair".
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "Ionic and covalent are unrelated" (1, 13); "1.7 is a sharp line" (8); "δ− on the less electronegative atom" (crossed in 15, site); "the ions stay in pairs" (18, handoff); "sodium and oxygen share" (crossed in 17).
- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m1-v22`; route handoff "Why do ionic solids conduct only when charge carriers can move?").** Scene 18: each Na⁺ attracts every Cl⁻ around it, so the ions build a regular pattern; why is that crystal hard, and why does it conduct only once it melts or dissolves? The chip uses v22's proposed question (v22 open decision 1). Final frame in its own section.
- **Site notes (read 5 November; for root to log in `../site-corrections-chem-y11.md` if accepted):**
  1. `l18-using-electronegativity-difference-to-classi-title` (and `-b`): the "< 0.4" row lists "CH₄ (Δχ=0.4)", while the next row is "0.4–1.7". 0.4 cannot sit in the "< 0.4" row. Suggest "CH₄ (C–H Δχ = 0.4, borderline; usually treated as non-polar)" and thresholds written "below about 0.4" and "about 0.4 to 1.7".
  2. Same table, ionic row: "KF (Δχ=3.3)" (already noted in v14, site note 1): 4.0 − 0.8 = 3.2 at one decimal; 3.98 − 0.82 = 3.16. Suggest 3.2.
  3. Activity 1(a): "H–F: |Δχ| = 4.0−2.2 = 1.8 ≥ 1.7 → ionic (or very strongly polar covalent ...)". The model answer should lead with "polar covalent (strongly polar); 1.8 is just above the 1.7 guide, but HF is molecular". Suggest reordering so "ionic" is not the first answer.
  4. Q7 model answer: "The bond is ionic/highly polar (at boundary)". Same point; suggest "strongly polar covalent".
  5. `l19-lewis-dot-diagrams-title`: "place the least electronegative atom in the centre" (step 2). Correct except hydrogen, which is never central. Suggest adding "(never hydrogen)". Minor.
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) atoms in a bond pull on the bonding electrons with a strength set by their electronegativity (2); (2) equal pull keeps a shared pair centred (3); (3) a larger difference pulls the pair toward one atom, giving partial charges (4); (4) a big enough difference moves the electron across, making ions, which attract (5); (5) so the bond type depends on the size of the difference, a spectrum (6); (6) elements far apart on the table differ most (6); (7) the guide values are approximate, so evidence decides near the boundary (8); (8) Lewis diagrams show which electrons move or are shared, and why the formula has its ratio (9 to 12).
- **Entry knowledge:** v14 (electronegativity, Pauling values, top-right trend, tug of war); v19 (ion charges, the noble gas arrangement, MgCl₂); v20 (ionic compounds made of ions; covalent compounds of atoms sharing electrons); v12 (valence electrons per group, used for Lewis dots).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary:** electronegativity difference (the larger value minus the smaller, 2); covalent bond (a pair of electrons shared between two atoms, recalled, 3); non-polar covalent bond (shared equally, 3); polar covalent bond (shared unequally, 4); δ+ and δ− (delta plus and delta minus: small partial charges, 4); ionic bond (the attraction between oppositely charged ions, 5); Lewis dot diagram (outer electrons drawn as dots around the symbol, 9); bonding pair and lone pair (a shared pair; a pair belonging to one atom only, 11); double bond (two shared pairs, 12).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded, plus plates):** **tug-of-war bond** (two nuclei with their shell rings, a grey rope line between them, and the bonding pair as two blue dots that slide along the rope according to Δχ; at Δχ about 2 or more the dots leave the rope and join the stronger atom's outer ring, the rope fades, and the two atoms gain "+" and "−" and attract with a soft pulse); **Δχ readout** (two value chips and a subtraction under the rope); **spectrum bar** (a horizontal bar from 0 to 3.3, with faint guide bands at 0.4 and 1.7 and example markers dropped onto it: Cl₂ 0, C–H 0.4, H–Cl 1.0, O–H 1.2, H–F 1.8, MgO 2.1, NaCl 2.3, KF 3.2); **periodic distance** (a coded periodic outline with two element boxes lit and a curved arrow between them whose length matches Δχ); **Lewis builder** (symbols with dots in pairs around four sides; the moving or shared electrons amber; brackets and charges write in; bonding pairs morph to a line); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Board layout (constant):** heading top left; the tug-of-war bond or Lewis diagram across the centre; Δχ readout under it; the spectrum bar along the lower third (above the caption-safe zone) once it exists.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Pauling electronegativities (PubChem, as v14 note a): F 3.98, O 3.44, Cl 3.16, N 3.04, Br 2.96, C 2.55, H 2.20, Mg 1.31, Na 0.93, K 0.82. One-decimal values match the site. Differences at one decimal (larger minus smaller): Cl–Cl 0, H–Cl 1.0, Na–Cl 2.3, H–F 1.8, K–Cl 2.4, N–H 0.8, Br–Br 0, Na–O 2.5, Mg–Cl 1.9, C–O 0.8, O–H 1.2, C–H 0.4, Mg–O 2.1, K–F 3.2. With full values: H–Cl 0.96, Na–Cl 2.23, H–F 1.78, K–Cl 2.34, N–H 0.84, Na–O 2.51, Mg–Cl 1.85, C–O 0.89, C–H 0.35; none changes a classification used here. MgCl₂ (1.9, at one decimal) is ionic by the guide and in practice; not shown as a Δχ.
(b) HF boils at 19.5 °C (CRC); NaCl melts at 801 °C. HF exists as hydrogen-bonded molecules; learner copy says only "made of separate molecules".
(c) The guide values 0.4 and 1.7 vary between textbooks (some use 0.5 and 2.0, or 1.8); the site's values are used. Learner copy says "as a rough guide" and "about".
(d) Lewis structures here obey the octet (duet for H). Expanded octets (PCl₅, SF₆ from v20) and formal charge are not drawn; v20's names stand without structures.
(e) The ionic Lewis diagram is a model of electron transfer; in reality ionic compounds form a lattice (v22), not ion pairs. Scene 18 says so.
(f) Pronunciations: "electronegativity" (ee-LEK-troh-neg-a-TIV-it-ee); "delta"; "Lewis" (LOO-iss); "non-polar" (non-POH-ler).

Main question: *How does electron attraction connect ionic and covalent bonding?*
Entry knowledge: v12, v14, v19, v20.
Stops after: Δχ and the spectrum, non-polar, polar and ionic bonds, δ+ and δ−, the HF boundary case, periodic positions, Lewis diagrams for NaCl, MgCl₂, H₂O and CO₂. No lattice, shapes, polar molecules, metallic bonding or intermolecular forces.
Handoff: chem-y11-m1-v22, the ionic lattice and its properties.

## Script and shots

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour key (continues v14 and v19): nuclei red; electrons blue; the moving or shared electrons in Lewis diagrams amber; rope line grey; δ+ red and δ− blue (small italic); ion charges teal; spectrum bar from grey (covalent end) to teal (ionic end) with faint guide bands; crossed chips red strike. Screen notation: Δχ (with the word "difference" beside it the first time), δ+, δ−, [Na]⁺, [Cl]⁻ with eight dots.

- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m1-v22`; route handoff "Why do ionic solids conduct only when charge carriers can move?").** Scene 18: each Na⁺ attracts every Cl⁻ around it, so the ions build a regular pattern; why is that crystal hard, and why does it conduct only once it melts or dissolves? The chip uses v22's proposed question (v22 open decision 1). Final frame in its own section.
- **Site notes (read 5 November; for root to log in `../site-corrections-chem-y11.md` if accepted):**

  5. `l19-lewis-dot-diagrams-title`: "place the least electronegative atom in the centre" (step 2). Correct except hydrogen, which is never central. Suggest adding "(never hydrogen)". Minor.
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) atoms in a bond pull on the bonding electrons with a strength set by their electronegativity (2); (2) equal pull keeps a shared pair centred (3); (3) a larger difference pulls the pair toward one atom, giving partial charges (4); (4) a big enough difference moves the electron across, making ions, which attract (5); (5) so the bond type depends on the size of the difference, a spectrum (6); (6) elements far apart on the table differ most (6); (7) the guide values are approximate, so evidence decides near the boundary (8); (8) Lewis diagrams show which electrons move or are shared, and why the formula has its ratio (9 to 12).
- **Entry knowledge:** v14 (electronegativity, Pauling values, top-right trend, tug of war); v19 (ion charges, the noble gas arrangement, MgCl₂); v20 (ionic compounds made of ions; covalent compounds of atoms sharing electrons); v12 (valence electrons per group, used for Lewis dots).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary:** electronegativity difference (the larger value minus the smaller, 2); covalent bond (a pair of electrons shared between two atoms, recalled, 3); non-polar covalent bond (shared equally, 3); polar covalent bond (shared unequally, 4); δ+ and δ− (delta plus and delta minus: small partial charges, 4); ionic bond (the attraction between oppositely charged ions, 5); Lewis dot diagram (outer electrons drawn as dots around the symbol, 9); bonding pair and lone pair (a shared pair; a pair belonging to one atom only, 11); double bond (two shared pairs, 12).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded, plus plates):** **tug-of-war bond** (two nuclei with their shell rings, a grey rope line between them, and the bonding pair as two blue dots that slide along the rope according to Δχ; at Δχ about 2 or more the dots leave the rope and join the stronger atom's outer ring, the rope fades, and the two atoms gain "+" and "−" and attract with a soft pulse); **Δχ readout** (two value chips and a subtraction under the rope); **spectrum bar** (a horizontal bar from 0 to 3.3, with faint guide bands at 0.4 and 1.7 and example markers dropped onto it: Cl₂ 0, C–H 0.4, H–Cl 1.0, O–H 1.2, H–F 1.8, MgO 2.1, NaCl 2.3, KF 3.2); **periodic distance** (a coded periodic outline with two element boxes lit and a curved arrow between them whose length matches Δχ); **Lewis builder** (symbols with dots in pairs around four sides; the moving or shared electrons amber; brackets and charges write in; bonding pairs morph to a line); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, `PenArrow`, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.

scenes.teachingReason: Last time, we named sodium chloride as ions, and carbon dioxide as atoms sharing electrons. But these aren't two separate worlds. Remember our tug of war from the electronegativity video, with two atoms pulling on a shared pair of electrons. If the pull is even, the pair stays in the middle. If one atom pulls harder, the pair shifts toward it. And if one atom pulls much, much harder, it can take the electrons completely. Let's see how that one idea connects covalent and ionic bonding.

scenes.teachingReason: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom in a bond attracts the shared electrons. It rises toward the top right of the periodic table. Fluorine is the highest, at four point zero. Chlorine is three point two, hydrogen two point two, and sodium only zero point nine. What decides the bond is the difference between the two atoms' values.

scenes.teachingReason: So bonding is a spectrum, not two boxes. As the difference grows, the shared pair moves further toward one atom, until it's handed over. As a rough guide, a difference below about zero point four is non-polar covalent. Between zero point four and one point seven is polar covalent. And above about one point seven is ionic. You can see it on the periodic table, too. A metal from the bottom left, with a non-metal from the top right, are far apart in electronegativity, so they bond ionically. Two non-metals, close together, share electrons.

scenes.teachingReason: For sodium oxide, oxygen has six outer electrons, and needs two more. Each sodium gives one. So there are two sodium ions in brackets, each plus one, and one oxide ion with eight dots, and a charge of minus two. For ammonia, nitrogen has five outer electrons. It shares one pair with each of three hydrogens, which leaves one lone pair. Drawing sodium and oxygen sharing a pair is the trap. A big electronegativity difference means transfer.

scenes.teachingReason: One last thing. In a real crystal of salt, each sodium ion doesn't pair up with just one chloride. It attracts every chloride ion around it, and each chloride attracts the sodiums around it, building a huge, regular pattern. So why is that crystal so hard, and why does it carry electricity only once it melts or dissolves? That's next time.

### 19. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".
> Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

1. Electronegativity difference (Δχ = larger − smaller) decides the bond. Bonding is a spectrum: below about 0.4 non-polar covalent (Cl₂, 0); about 0.4 to 1.7 polar covalent (H–Cl, 1.0); above about 1.7 ionic (NaCl, 2.3). The values are a guide (HF, 1.8, is molecular).
2. Polar covalent: δ− on the more electronegative atom, δ+ on the other. Ionic bond: the attraction between oppositely charged ions after electron transfer.
3. Lewis dot diagrams show outer electrons only. Ionic: [Na]⁺ [:Cl:]⁻, ions in brackets with charges. Covalent: bonding pairs (lines) and lone pairs; H₂O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs on O; CO₂ is O=C=O.

Memory aid (large, on the notes screen): *Small gap, share. Big gap, transfer.*
